Stipend Vs. Contract: Which is Appropriate?

From the ORA eTraining module "Supporting Participants: Payments, Benefits, and Indirect Costs" (lesson 2 of 9).
Employee Contract vs. Participant Stipend
Employee
Employment Contract An employment contract is used when the institution pays an employee for work on a sponsored project, such as salary, wages, or summer research contracts. The core idea is compensation for services rendered. Under Uniform Guidance ( 2 CFR 200.430 ), this is employee compensation and is tied to actual work benefiting the award. Hallmarks of a Contract There is a defined service, deliverable, or work expectation. Pay is tied to the work being performed. Documentation often includes scope of work or position description, dates, pay rate, deliverables, approvals, and payment terms. Employee pay usually carries payroll treatment and associated fringe benefit charges.
Participant
Stipend Support A stipend is not pay for services. It is subsistence support given to a participant, fellow, or trainee so they can take part in training or another eligible educational activity. Uniform Guidance includes stipends within participant support costs, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) states directly that stipends support living expenses during training and are not employee compensation. The National Science Foundation (NSF) similarly describes participants as people whose primary purpose is learning or receiving training and who receive a stipend rather than salary and fringe benefits. Hallmarks of a Stipend The primary purpose is training or participation, not labor. The amount is often predetermined. It is not based on hours worked. It is not paid in exchange for institutional services like staffing a lab, entering data, coordinating recruitment, or managing project operations. It is only appropriate when the sponsor and the award purpose allow it. At institutes of higher education (IHEs), federal rules say scholarships, fellowships, and student aid are allowable only when the award’s purpose is to provide training to participants and the agency approves the cost.
Ask yourself this simple question: Are we paying this person because we need them to do work for the project, or because we are supporting them while they learn or participate? If the answer is do work , that points to a contract arrangement. If the answer is learn/participate/train , that points to a stipend arrangement.

Quick Guide: Stipend Vs. Contract
Question Contract Stipend Why are you paying them? To perform work or provide services To support training or participation Is labor expected? Yes No, not as employee services Tied to hours/tasks/deliverables? Usually yes Usually no Fringe benefits? Often yes for employees No, not as salary/fringe Allowable on any sponsored award? Potentially, if necessary, reasonable, allocable, and permitted Only when sponsor/award purpose permits training or participant support Typical examples Employee salary, GA wages, consultant agreement Trainee stipend, fellow stipend, workshop participant stipend
Knowledge Check Scenario
Scene 1
slide
Activity on Awards: Stipend v. Contract
In this scenario, we will test our understanding of when it is appropriate to use a stipend versus a contract for student time associated with sponsored projects.
Great job! This student is participating in a structured training and educational experience. The description emphasizes workshops, mentorship, guided learning, and program participation rather than assigned work duties performed for the benefit of the project. That makes stipend support the more appropriate option.
Stipend
tryAgain
disappointed
Oh no! A contract is generally more appropriate when an individual is being paid to perform work or provide services to the project. In this scenario, the student is described as a participant in a training program, not as someone carrying out operational or employment-like responsibilities.
Contract
Dr. Clark Kent is the PI of an NSF-funded summer research program at Morgan State University. One undergraduate student from another university will join the program for eight weeks, during which she will attend research training workshops, receive faculty mentorship, participate in guided learning activities, and present at the end-of-program showcase. Dr. Kent wants to use project funds to support her participation. Based on this information, should this support most appropriately be processed as a stipend or a contract?
neutral
end
Have you been paying attention? A stipend is generally appropriate when the individual is participating in a training, educational, or programmatic experience as a participant rather than performing work for the project. Here, the facts point more clearly to work responsibilities, so stipend support would not be the best fit.
Great work! In this version, the student is performing assigned duties that directly support the project’s operations. That points to compensation for services rendered rather than support for participation in a training experience.
Now assume the situation is slightly different. Instead of joining the project primarily as a trainee, the student will be responsible for assisting with project operations throughout the summer by organizing research files, maintaining project data, preparing materials for program activities, and completing other assigned tasks under the direction of Dr. Kent and project staff. Based on these revised details, should this support most appropriately be processed as a stipend or a contract?
